title: Conspiracy Beliefs, Misinformation, Social Media Platforms, and Protest Participation
screen_reason: The paper's aim is protest participation, but Table 1 (descriptive statistics by country) reports the share of respondents coded 1 on a self-report misinformation-exposure item ('In the past month, how often on social media have you seen someone share misinformation?'), for the pooled sample and for each of the four countries. That is a quantitative share of survey respondents reporting encountering misinformation, with the survey sample as denominator = RECALL (exposure). Belief-in-conspiracy items and all regression coefficients are not shares and are not extracted.

estimates.platform: social media (self-reported, platform not specified in the item)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents coded 1 on the recoded dummy for having seen someone share misinformation on social media in the past month
estimates.denominator: 1,500 US respondents in an online panel survey (Lightspeed Kantar Group, quotas matched to census)
estimates.definition: Respondent coded 1 on the dummy recoded from the frequency item 'In the past month, how often on social media have you seen someone share misinformation?'; the authors recoded the original response options into a 0/1 dummy but do not state the cut-point.
estimates.misinfo_def: "By misinformation, we mean false or misleading information."
estimates.source_quote: The next questions will ask about 0 or 1 70% 73% 67% 66% 74% misinformation on social media. By misinformation, we mean false or misleading information. In the past month, how often on social media have you seen someone share misinformation?
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-assessment against the survey's own wording ('false or misleading information'); no external verification. The authors flag this: "In this article, we rely on self-reported exposure to misinformation, which is a limitation. We do not know for certain if the respondents viewed misinformation on social media."
estimates.moderator_quote: For platform use, misinformation exposure, and ideology, we recoded the original response options to create dummy variables. The approach matches theories and existing research as well as addresses skewed response distributions.
estimates.notes: Percentage is verbatim from Table 1. Dummy cut-point on the underlying 'how often' scale is not reported, so the exact threshold for 'exposed' is unknown (hence medium confidence). Item asks about seeing someone SHARE misinformation, i.e. the respondent's own exposure, not the respondent's own sharing -> recall_subtype exposure.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The pooled 'All' value for the same item is 70% (6,068 respondents across the four countries). Not entered as a fifth row because it is the aggregate of the four country rows already extracted and would double-count the same respondents; adjudicators wanting one row per study should use 70% / n=6,068 (verbatim in Table 1, 'All' column). (2) Everything else in the paper is a regression coefficient, odds ratio or correlation (Tables 2-4), not a share, so nothing else is poolable: e.g. Misinformation ExpB = 1.41, p = 0.014 for protest participation. (3) Table 1 also gives platform-use shares (Twitch 18%, TikTok 25%, YouTube 86%, Facebook 80%) and protest-participation shares (11% any march; 3% left-wing, 4% right-wing protest) - these are not misinformation measures. (4) The conspiracy-belief measure is reported only as a scale mean (3.01 on 1-4), never as a share of respondents, and belief is excluded by the protocol anyway. (5) The dummy cut-point on the 'how often' scale is unstated; if an adjudicator requires an explicit threshold or an explicit 'any exposure' wording, these four rows would drop to borderline.

rob.design: Cross-national online panel survey fielded by Lightspeed Kantar Group in February 2021; n = 6,068 (Canada 1,568; UK 1,500; France 1,500; US 1,500) with quotas matched to national census composition; no response rate or panel-recruitment detail reported; misinformation exposure measured by a single self-report frequency item recoded to a 0/1 dummy with unstated cut-point (no reliability possible for a single item); conspiracy-belief scale reliability reported as 0.768 full sample (0.746 US, 0.772 UK, 0.756 France, 0.768 Canada); ethics file No. 101856; replication files posted on figshare.
